key_insight: When neural networks learn many tasks, they naturally split into specialized modules, especially when model capacity is limited. Training tasks incrementally makes this modular structure stronger and more similar to the organization of brain networks.
problem_solved: The paper addresses how multi-task learning systems can organize themselves efficiently without being manually designed, and whether the resulting structure resembles modular organization seen in the brain.
method: Train artificial neural networks on multiple tasks under different capacity constraints.
Compare network organization across training regimes, including incremental multitask learning.
Analyze emergent modularity and compare the resulting architectures with known brain network patterns.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests that modular architectures may emerge naturally from task structure and limited capacity, rather than needing to be imposed manually. It also points to training strategies that can improve specialization, efficiency, and biological plausibility.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram of a monolithic network versus a modular network
Flowchart showing multitask training leading to specialized modules
Heatmap or connectivity graph illustrating increasing modularity under capacity constraints
Brain network comparison panel showing similarity between artificial and biological architectures
paper_title: Task-structured modularity emerges in artificial networks and aligns with brain architecture
paper_authors: Yuhang Wu, Shikuang Deng, Kangrui Du, Marcelo G. Mattar, Yifan Wu
